title: A Performance-Weighted Environmental Assessment of Ultra-High-Volume Fly Ash Substitution in Portland Cement Concrete
content: Portland cement concrete (PCC) production accounts for a significant share of global CO₂ emissions but fly ash substitution for cement remains constrained by concerns over mechanical performance at high replacement rates. This study evaluates PCC mixes incorporating fly ash Type C (FA-C) or Type F (FA-F) across cement replacement rates from 10% to 90%, tracking fresh-state workability, compressive strength, and surface electrical resistivity at 7, 14, and 28 curing days. A process-based life cycle assessment (LCA) with the TRACI 2.1 method quantified global warming potential (GWP, kg CO₂/m³) under a raw-material-plus-batching-electricity boundary for each mix. A Performance Index (PI) that normalizes GWP by compressive strength and electrical resistivity provided a performance-weighted environmental efficiency metric. A sensitivity analysis across different weights tested the robustness of mix rankings under varying priorities for structural versus durability performance, and a structural threshold analysis identified mixes meeting strength requirements. Contrary to conventional expectations, FA-C at 50% cement replacement exceeded the OPC control in 28-day compressive strength (42.9 vs. 36.2 MPa) and electrical resistivity (9.88 vs. 8.50 kΩ·cm), while reducing GWP by 48.3% relative to the OPC control (40.24 kg CO₂/m³). The GWP/PI metric revealed that raw GWP reduction alone misrepresents environmental efficiency: mixes achieving the greatest GWP reductions at ultra-high replacement rates incur disproportionate performance penalties that offset their environmental gains when normalized. FA-C at 50% achieved a GWP/PI of 17.73 (α = 0.5), which is a 56% improvement over the OPC control. These findings challenge the conventional <30% substitution ceiling and demonstrate that performance-weighted LCA metrics provide a more informed basis for sustainable concrete mix design.
